And then compared to kids with Down syndrome alone, those who have both can have some differences as well. So it's really important that a specialist with experience diagnosing these is involved, again, as soon as that autism diagnosis is suspected. Because really earlier treatment is important for all children with autism, including those with Down syndrome. And then I wanted to highlight kind of the last piece on the autism front is the Down syndrome autism connection, which is a great resource for families who have children with that dual diagnosis. It was founded in 2007. So it's a longstanding organization. And again, really beneficial from families. So check it out if that fits with you. For the diagnosis of acute regression, there was some research published that our team was part of. And we have a different kind of checklist format of showing all the different components that could go along with this regression. So things like changes in adaptive function, like needing more help to do activities of daily living, changes in speech, changes in social skills. But all of that's listed in the checklist if you have any worries that either your patient or your loved one with Down syndrome might have acute regression. And there are also new consensus criteria that were published that go through the different medical features. And then there are different kind of cutoffs for those where either DSRD, Down syndrome regression disorder is possible or probable, depending on the number of symptoms that one has. And then additionally, for those who were wondering about acute regression, as I mentioned, it's really a multidisciplinary approach with a tiered medical workup, wanting to look for any medical conditions that could either mimic or worsen those symptoms of regression. Okay, so now I'll just quickly turn to adult health care for a bit. I wanted to highlight again, adults with Down syndrome are often more like adults without Down syndrome than they are different. So anything that you typically recommend for an adult without Down syndrome, it's probably a great idea for adults with Down syndrome too, like, you know, getting regular screenings, getting all their immunizations, staying up to date on their routine health maintenance, and a lot of kind of the typical rapport building and relationship building that physicians and adults with Down syndrome would benefit from. And then there were adult-specific health guidelines published in 2020 for adults with Down syndrome. Again, Down syndrome is quite common, but when we reviewed the literature, we found that there really is not a ton of evidence to guide these evidence-based clinical practice guidelines. So the way it worked, there was a 13-member work group with a 29-member committee. So I always have to share that, you know, this was really the work of a lot of different people. I was lucky to be one of the volunteer authors for one section, but I really played a small role in this kind of big effort that was led by the Global Down syndrome Foundation. And at the end of their guidelines, they have a summary table that shows the different components that are recommended for different ages. And I know this is small, but just wanting to show you kind of the breadth and the amount of screening that should be done at different times based on the different kind of eight health topics that they looked at here. And overall, from this review, they came up with 14 recommendations and four statements of good practice for healthcare of adults with Down syndrome. And so the one strong recommendation was to screen for Alzheimer's type dementia, beginning at age 40 for adults with Down syndrome. A couple of recommendations about diabetes screening. And then four recommendations, you can see the topics listed here, where the evidence basically agreed with the existing guidance for individuals without Down syndrome. And so just to summarize here, this is the piece about Alzheimer's dementia, the different scales or different topics that are recommended to be screened for, like cognition, like cognition, memory, executive function, behavior, personality, communication, adaptive function, ambulation and motor skills, and general decline in established skills. And then this is the specific kind of text or guidance about screening for diabetes. And for asymptomatic adults, meaning without co-occurring obesity, they recommend screening for type 2 diabetes using a hemoglobin A1c or a fasting plasma glucose every three years, beginning at age 30. And then for adults with Down syndrome and obesity. And then for adults with Down syndrome and obesity, they recommend screening for type 2 diabetes using hemoglobin A1c every two to three years, beginning at age 21. So just a bit earlier, I'm just reading that because the text is hard to see. So just so you have the ages there, 30 and 21 for adults with Down syndrome. And then I think it's really important when you're seeing patients with Down syndrome in clinic or, you know, when you're meeting with a medical professional. I really think medical professionals should treat each person like an individual to know that there's a range of communication skills in Down syndrome. Often visual skills are a strength. And then talking always to the person with Down syndrome is ideal. Sometimes folks with Down syndrome need a bit more time to communicate, to express themselves. So just having that patience and being willing to kind of meet their skills where they are and being nonjudgmental in working with patients with Down syndrome. And I think your perspective really matters. You know, if you know people with Down syndrome or have folks in your community, I think that really goes a long way for medical professionals to have that experience and comfort of working with them in clinic. And I wanted to talk about this new Down syndrome health measure that we developed through research. But I'll be sharing a bit of background about how we developed it and the research that went into creating it. So I mentioned these health supervision guidelines for children and adolescents with Down syndrome. We talked about some of the components and how they've existed. But in the process of doing this research, I had a really smart reviewer ask me a tough question. So that led me to a new project. This was a career mentored research award from the National Institutes of Health that I started in 2020. And we really thought about, again, what is health to you? What defines how healthy you are? What are indicators or signs that you're in good health? And overall, we often kept thinking, you know, that this could be different for each person, that people could have a diagnosis and still feel healthy if that diagnosis was managed or treated well. You know, thinking of something like diabetes or hypertension, you know, you can have those, but still be in good health if you're taking the right steps to kind of manage it. So we started with the World Health Organization definition of health, which has these three main dimensions, physical, social and mental well-being. And we really liked this one because we said it wasn't just the absence of disease. Again, you can have a disease, you can have a diagnosis and still feel healthy. For instance, important things like medication management, paying bills or balancing a checkbook, grocery shopping and cooking regular meals, making and keeping appointments, and challenges with driving. Sometimes there might be a new fender bender or missing a sign. There are several types of dementia. So when we think of dementia, a healthcare provider will think of this list. Alzheimer's disease, cerebrovascular disease, Lewy body disease, Parkinson's, frontal temporal dementia. So dementia is an all-encompassing term that can be caused by any one of these things. Alzheimer's in particular is really important because it's the majority of cases of dementia. Cerebrovascular disease is a dementia related to years of elevated blood pressure and cholesterol. And oftentimes somebody with cerebrovascular disease might have a step-wise decline. They're fine and then they're not. They're fine for a while and then they're not. Lewy body disease is noted for people with sleep disturbances like sleep wake cycles or bad dreams. They might have hallucinations or difficulty with visual spatial and executive functions. Executive functions meaning things like multitasking and planning and executing. People with dementia related to Parkinson's disease, I've actually had Parkinson's for more than a year. Frontotemporal dementia is demonstrated when people have significant personality or behavior disorders. And then there's a common term called mixed dementia, which can be a combination of any of these. When testing for cognitive impairment and evaluating that, there's the medical informant, the physician talking to the patient, but also the informant interview where the physician will, hopefully a care partner or loved one has come to the appointment and they also can share their perspective on how things are going at home. And some of the things that people will ask in that evaluation are ADLs, which stands for activity of daily living. These are the things that you need to get up and get out of the house on a daily basis, getting dressed, bathing, toileting, grooming and eating. We also are curious about the instrumental activities of daily living, things that are a little bit more complex that you need in your daily living. In order to get through a week, like shopping, cooking, cleaning, laundry, finances and transportation. Usually if someone's getting an evaluation for memory, they'll actually have a memory test in clinic. There are two popular ones that we use. One is called the Montreal Cognitive Assessment Test or MOCA, and then there's the RUDIS, the Ralland Universal Dementia Assessment. Oftentimes the MOCA is used as a first choice just because it's more commonly used, but if there are differences in language, particularly if English is not somebody's native language, we'll choose the RUDIS. Or if somebody has not made it through high school, we'll choose the RUDIS. As the name indicates, it's a little bit more universal. And in these memory tests, there are certain domains which we think about how someone's brain works or their cognition. At testing, excuse me, testing attention and concentration, language, calculation, executive function, which is the multitasking and planning I mentioned, memory, visual spatial skills and orientation, meaning what day is it, where are we, that kind of thing. And let's recall for a moment the fact that these items interfere with our memory, so we'll ask questions about those too. Sleep, mood and stress, medication, the need for hearing aids, under or untreated medical problems and tobacco and alcohol. Sometimes at this point, you have a sense, you know why someone's not doing well. They're sleeping two hours a night, or they're severely depressed, or they're on a medication like Tylenol PM, so the Benadryl in the PM is really messing up how they're thinking and being able to perform. So not everybody needs to go beyond this step. Perhaps this is where we stop, fix and then reassess. Oops, excuse me. But if there's, we don't have a clear answer, I'm gonna go back for a second. A BMP is a basic metabolic panel, which is your sodium, potassium, glucose and kidney function. And LFT, which is liver function tests. Sometimes imaging is needed. And then also one thing that we're all very interested in is volume loss. Because as I mentioned earlier, our brain shrinks. We wanna see if this shrinkage is appropriate for someone's age. And there are several phases of dementia and one is a newly appreciated phase called the preclinical phase. And it's considered preclinical because people or somebody with evidence of neurofibrillary tangles and amyloid plaques isn't showing any signs of memory impairment. They're able to perform their tasks at work and at home and nobody is the wiser that something's going on. Then there are, then if Alzheimer's has been diagnosed, as we mentioned earlier, memory impairment that prevents somebody from managing independently, there will be a mild, moderate and severe in stage disease. The symptoms of Alzheimer's disease and also some of the other dementias can be apathy and or depression, apathy where somebody's not as interested in what they used to do, whether it's a hobby or a TV show or just going out having coffee with friends or just like, I don't know, I just don't feel like it. That's apathy or depression, I think we all can recognize what depression is and that can be an early sign of Alzheimer's disease. People can have increased anxiety, partially because there's this sense that something's not going right and just don't know what it is and that makes people more anxious. Also the idea that just increased anxiety can be a feature. Forgetfulness, trouble with word finding, trouble with short-term memory, meaning you've just told somebody the appointments at three o'clock and then five minutes later, what's the appointment? And then missing social cues, maybe subtle hints that someone's, suggesting that we do or don't do something or imagine you're at a cocktail party and someone's like, no, don't say anything. And you sort of miss that clue too. So these can be kind of non-specific, very common in any of the dementias. So this would be an early sign. As dementia progresses, there can be problems with general routines and routines and things that seem like simple tasks, like getting dressed. Sometimes a shirt will be put on inside out or the button's wrong or one layer over top, another that isn't quite right. There can be weight loss because people forget to eat, they don't recognize that they're as hungry, maybe they've forgotten how to prepare something, even like a peanut butter and jelly sandwich. So weight loss is another feature and falls due to inattention, usually. Disrupted sleep wake cycle is something that's really important. As we mentioned earlier, sleep can interfere with memory. And then when we do develop a dementia, sometimes people just have, they need more tired during the day and want to take a nap and then the nap sort of rob somebody of their consolidated sleep at nighttime. Or if any of you out there know somebody with dementia where they begin to wander and fiddle and do those kinds of things, really when they should be asleep. So a disturbed sleep wake cycle is definitely a feature. Then there's also hallucinations or delusions. Hallucination is seeing or hearing something that's not there. For instance, sometimes people can see little children or little animals in the room or maybe even a relative that's passed away. A delusion is confusing something that really is there with something else. For instance, a coat rack might appear, with a coat hanging on it, might appear like a man. So that's a delusion. I had a patient the other day in clinic who has hydrangea, the shrub in her yard and the ball of the hydrangea, she thought was a person. She thought that was a face. And then there's paranoia where you're worried that somebody's entering the house or that somebody's out to get you or that there's some infidelity with the spouse. So these would be along the lines of moderate dementia. And so how do we treat this? Dementia, first of all, is really hard to treat. It's really hard to treat. It's a challenge for obviously family members, but it is also for the medical community. We have this class of medication called colonesterase inhibitors, which might be familiar to some of you. Dinepazil or erycept is one of the standard medications we try. There's also rivastigmine and galantamine. And these medications are used to try to slow down the progression of the disease. Imagine there's a slope of a line or an angle like in a triangle. And if this is the normal trajectory of memory loss, we try to flatten it out just a little bit so our endpoint might take, we might get to the same endpoint, but a little bit longer. Common side effects of these medications are abdominal pain, then leading to weight loss, and also a slower heart rate. So if somebody has, whose blood pressure or heart rate is a little on the low side to begin with, I might forego this medicine. As mentioned earlier, one of the things that can mimic dementia and also be an early feature of dementia is depression or anxiety. And sometimes, in fact, oftentimes a physician or a nurse practitioner might start an SSRI or an anti-depression or anti-anxiety medication, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor medication. To see if treating the dementia or, sorry, treating the depression or the anxiety might improve the memory and the functioning. These are the three medicines that the geriatrician would approve of. As Amy mentioned, I'm a geriatrician. Nutrition and cancer care. If you've attended any of our previous webinars through the Blum Center, we've primarily focused on managing the side effects of cancer and its treatment. And today's topic really enters the realm of nutrition for wellness and survivorship. And during active treatment for cancer, our primary goals as registered dietitians are to help patients with weight maintenance, preservation of lean body mass, and symptom management in order to optimize tolerance of treatment and improve quality of life. So, specific guidance for managing malnutrition, poor appetite, nausea, taste changes, and difficulty swallowing is currently available on the Blum Center's YouTube page in case anyone would like more information about these topics. For cancer survivorship, we draw many of our recommendations from the American Institute for Cancer Research and the World Cancer Research Fund. We have identified 10 pillars for the prevention of cancer and its recurrence, and six of these pillars are specifically about nutrition. The first nutrition related pillar is to eat a diet rich in whole grains, vegetables, fruit, and beans. So these foods should ideally form the bulk of the diet. Practically, I tell patients to aim for about five half cup servings of fruits and vegetables daily and then weave in whole grains and plant proteins throughout the meals they're having. So for example, if we're thinking about whole grains that might look like oatmeal at breakfast, whole wheat bread at lunch, and then some sort of grain as a side at dinner like bulgur, farro, quinoa, etc. Then the next pillar is to limit consumption of fast foods and other items high in primarily saturated fat, starches, or sugars. So these would be items to consume infrequently. Then they recommend that patients limit consumption of bread and processed meat. I usually tell patients if they do consume red meat to try to limit it to about a serving a week and avoid processed meat as much as possible. Next is to limit consumption of sugar, sweetened drinks and try to consume more plain water or seltzer if carbonation is enjoyable. Then limit alcohol consumption. This recommendation is because the body metabolizes alcohol into a compound called acid aldehyde that can cause DNA damage. And then finally, they state do not use supplements for cancer prevention. Ideally, supplements would be used to correct a nutrient deficiency, support bone health, or supplement certain dietary patterns. For example, a vegan diet may require certain supplementation. And I also want to note on this point that there is no supplement known to prevent cancer or it's recurrence. In terms of the survivorship recommendations, our colleagues Ashley Dravium and Carol Sullivan recently gave an excellent talk through the Blum Center called paving the way with every bite nutrition as a tool for cancer survivorship. And that provides a deep dive into these pillars, as well as specific ideas for how to implement them. I believe that talk is also now available on the Blum Center YouTube page if anyone is interested to learn more. There are many reasons why heart health is particularly important for people with a history of cancer. Cancer and cardiovascular disease share a number of risk factors and mechanisms, including oxidative stress and inflammation. The key takeaways here are that people with a history of cancer have a significantly increased risk of cardiovascular disease compared to the general population. And this risk is largely attributed to treatment toxicity. Emerging research also suggests that a history of cardiovascular disease may influence the risk of developing cancer. And so this image summarizes that potential bidirectional link. On a bright note, lifestyle behaviors are some of the best ways to prevent cardiovascular disease. So what does that look like? In terms of nutrition, the American Heart Association recommends a diet that emphasizes a variety of fruits, vegetables and whole grains. And this is a diet that focuses on healthy protein sources. So that will primarily be lean animal proteins like fish, seafood and poultry that is unprocessed, as well as plant sources of proteins like legumes and nuts. And then there is the encouraged consumption of liquid non-tropical vegetable oils. So these are really going to be your heart healthy unsaturated fats, things that are liquid at room temperature. Minimal processed foods, minimal added sugars specifically for men. The American Heart Association suggests limiting added sugars to 36 grams or about nine teaspoons a day. And for women, that recommendation is a limit of 25 grams or about six teaspoons a day. And added sugars will be listed on all food labels. Additionally, encourage minimal salt, usually a maximum of about 2300 milligrams daily, and then limited or preferably no alcohol. Other lifestyle considerations include regular exercise. They specifically suggest two and a half hours of moderate or 75 minutes of vigorous physical activity each week. And then they recommend that people avoid tobacco products, get adequate sleep, achieve and maintain a healthy weight, which is going to look different person to person, and manage cholesterol, blood sugar and blood pressure. And those targets will likely be individualized as well based on guidance from healthcare providers. Now let's put this information together. It may already be clear that the survivorship and heart health guidelines are almost identical regarding nutrition. The key overlaps are to eat a predominantly plant based diet, focus on lean protein sources, limit calories from saturated fat. This, we didn't get into two specifically early on, but the American Heart Association specifically suggests that less than 6% of total calories, which is about 13 grams of saturated fat on a 2000 calorie diet, come from saturated fat. So, to provide an example of what that might look like on a plate, that's about a six ounce rib by a steak, a tablespoon of coconut oil, or two or three slices of full fat cheese for the whole day. I included here a picture of the new American plate, which the American Institute for Cancer Research created, because I think this provides a helpful visual to put this guidance into an actual meal. The idea is that this framework can be applied to all meals for the day. So for example at breakfast, that might be an omelet with eggs as the animal protein, but then including a bunch of vegetables as well. During active cancer treatment, guidance may vary. So first, certain cancer types and treatment regimens are associated with what's known as a state of hyper metabolism during which the body's energy and protein needs increase significantly. Patients with hyper metabolism may need to eat a lot more than usual simply to maintain their body weight. And in this case, it might be easier to consume calories from dietary fat and fluids. Certainly if people can start with heart healthy fats like olive oil and avocado. That's an ideal calorie booster. But some people may need butter, ice cream, full fat dairy products and sugar sweetened beverages, which are quite caloric in order to prioritize weight maintenance and that is okay. Eating during active treatment is all about balancing priorities. In terms of fiber, tolerance might vary, particularly if someone has GI issues such as constipation or diarrhea. And finally, physical activity is typically at the discretion of each patient's treatment team, people recovering from surgery or with other specific contraindications may need to take it easy. So I want to provide some more specific guidance around protein. On active treatment, 1.2 to 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight is typically adequate to maintain muscle mass. And we encourage people to choose well tolerated protein sources. So that's really going to be any protein food that appeals and doesn't cause GI upset. So for some people, 1.2 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight is typically adequate, but this of course varies based on age, medical history, personal goals and activity levels. So for someone who's very active and trying to rebuild muscle, they may need a bit more than that. And again, the focus should be on trying to get protein from lean and plant based sources. The thing about long-term care insurance is that they become prohibitively expensive if you're actually trying to start getting them later in your life. They really are things that people should start getting in their 40s and 50s and not later because they become extremely expensive as we age. That being said, if you do have long-term care insurance, it's important to look at a few things. First of all is when they can be activated and what kind of services they support. Most can be activated when you have needs both with what we call instrumental activities of daily living, things like shopping, household cleaning, that kind of thing. And most especially when you have more basic needs around walking, dressing, bathing, etc. But each plan is slightly different. So first is to look at when they can be activated. And the activation process is usually a process. It's not just a one-and-done situation. And then the second is how long are they for? And a lot of times when the person gets long-term care insurance, they go through an actuarial process where someone decides that they will experience some need for functional support over three years or five years. And it's not uncommon for long-term care policies to only last for like three to seven years. So you want to be aware of A, how long it can last, B, how when someone can activate it, and then C, can you turn it on and off? So for example, if you have a three-year policy, can you use it for six months and stop and then start it back again? Or is it a continuous? And these are the things that I found in talking to colleagues who've been thinking about their own policies or whether not to get policies or whether not to activate their policies often run up against. So that's my short answer to what could be probably an hour-long conversation about long-term care insurance. So to get to tonight's speaker, Robert Goldstein is the commissioner of the Massachusetts Department of Public Health. He was appointed the commissioner by Governor Maura Healy in April of 2023. He specializes in infectious diseases and he oversees a workforce of more than 3,200 people committed to health equity and dedicated to promoting the health and well-being of people across Massachusetts, preventing illness and injury and maintaining strong and vibrant communities. This work is carried out through a network of bureaus and offices responsible for priorities that include maternal and child health, nutrition, infectious diseases, injury prevention, climate and environmental health, substance use disorders, emergency preparedness and response, and problem gambling. Also, the DPH licenses health professionals in healthcare facilities and operates the state public health lab and four public health hospitals. Dr. Goldstein previously served as senior policy advisor at the CDC where he focused on public health emergency response, infectious diseases, and strategic policy initiatives. Before his work at the CDC, he founded and was the medical director of the Massachusetts General Hospital Transgender Health Program, a clinical resource offering a safe and affirming environment for the transgender and non-binary community. His clinical interest involved caring for those living with and at risk for HIV, an experience that continues to drive his passion to identify and eliminate barriers to equitable access to care. And lastly, he's a graduate of Tufts University where he also earned both his MD and his PhD. With that, let's welcome Dr. Goldstein. Dr. Goldstein. Dr. Goldstein. Good evening, everyone. And thank you, Sarah, for that very generous and very long introduction. Thank you to the Russell Museum for hosting this conversation. Dr. Goldstein. This space is special. This is a place that tells the rich history of medicine, a place that reminds me of my own history in medicine. It quite literally surrounds us with the history of medicine, and perhaps more importantly, the history of courage in medicine. It is deeply personal for me to stand here tonight. I trained in internal medicine in this hospital. I walked these hallways as an infectious disease fellow and as an attending physician. I saw patients here. I learned from extraordinary nurses, social workers, administrators, support staff, trainees, and inspiring attending physicians right here at Mass General. What I learned and experienced here shaped me as a physician. It shaped me as a person. Yes, I learned how to diagnose and treat disease, and that is the explicit curriculum of training at Mass General. But what I also witnessed here, the hidden curriculum, was how healthcare is inseparable from fairness, from dignity, from equity, and from justice. What I learned here is foundational to my understanding of public health. It's what public health is all about. It is medicine, in its broadest sense, practice at scale, for everyone, equitably. For more than 250 years, starting before this nation was born, before this hospital opened its doors to patients, Massachusetts has served as a laboratory for discovery. It's never been about medicine alone. It's also about the bold, and sometimes uncomfortable, idea that society has a responsibility to protect health collectively. It's about the people, and about choices, often made in moments of uncertainty and challenge. And these moments ripple outward in ways we could never have predicted. And it's also about courage. So tonight, I want to talk about public health through the lens of both the Commonwealth and the MGH. This is not a history lecture. It's a story about continuity, about how the questions we wrestle with today—trust, equity, fear, science, politics—are not new. What I want to explore with you is what this long and fascinating history of public health can teach us about how we move forward. And I want to begin this journey before public health even had a name, before it was a formal discipline, but not before it existed in practice. In 1721, Boston was gripped by a devastating smallpox outbreak. At the time, disease was widely understood as fate, as something to endure rather than to prevent. But that year, an extraordinary exchange of knowledge changed history. The well-known and widely respected Puritan minister Cotton Mather learned from an enslaved man in his household named Onesimus about a practice used in West Africa. Onesimus himself had undergone this practice, which involved introducing the material from a smallpox sore into a cut in his skin, causing a milder form of smallpox, and then providing lifelong protection against the disease. This wasn't a laboratory discovery. It wasn't science as we define it today. This was lived experience. It was knowledge carried across an ocean in the body of someone who had been unwillingly enslaved. It was knowledge Onesimus willingly shared to help others. Fascinated by the story, Mather, a minister, a man of God, viewed the knowledge as divine intervention. He wrote to a group of 14 Boston physicians, imploring them to try inoculation as a way to protect the population. Only one physician had the courage to step forward. That was Dr. Zabdiel Boylston. Dr. Boylston began cautiously. He inoculated his own young son, a decision that reflected both scientific curiosity and personal bravery. He inoculated two enslaved people in his house. And then he continued inoculating patients, despite fierce and vicious backlash. The practice was condemned by the Boston Town Council as widely criticized by clergy and physicians as reckless, dangerous, and ungodly. But Mather and Boylston were repeatedly threatened for these actions. Yet the results that eventually emerged were striking. For the nearly 250 people Boylston inoculated, the mortality rate was below 2%, dramatically lower than the death rate among those who had acquired smallpox naturally. And those inoculated were spared the disfiguring lifelong scars and other lasting effects of the horrific disease. Dr. Boylston completed what we would now define as a cohort study. It was one of the earliest examples of using comparative data to evaluate a medical intervention. Support for inoculation was slow to catch on. It gradually did, though. Fear and controversy about the practice dragged on for decades. And this moment revealed something important and enduring. Public health innovation often begins at the intersection of lived experience, scientific curiosity, and moral courage. And new ideas almost always faced resistance at the outset. Connie Mather, Onesimus, and Dr. Boylston were pioneering in the first half of the 18th century. Despite their work, smallpox inoculation was still a controversial practice in 1775, when the Revolutionary War broke out here in Massachusetts. Around that same time, another smallpox outbreak was brewing in the colonies. The disease affected the Continental Army. In fact, more soldiers were dying from disease than from enemy bullets. In 1777, General George Washington made a decision that may have been one of the most consequential public health actions in American history. He weighed the evidence, he listened to the physicians, and he mandated smallpox inoculation for all soldiers who had not had the disease previously. This was not a popular decision. It was politically risky, militarily uncertain, but it was decisive. And it worked. The decision protected the Continental Army, and likely was a major factor in the birth of our nation. General George Washington implemented our nation's first vaccination requirement, the first vaccine mandate. He did so with courage, and he demonstrated in his actions something that reverberates through generations. The act of public health is, in so many ways, an act of patriotism. More than two decades later, Boston would take another decisive step in the arc of public health. In 1799, the city of Boston created the first municipal public health board in the United States. Its president, Paul Revere. Yes, that Paul Revere, the midnight writer who warned the townspeople about the arrival of the British troops, the same Boston patriot who had a thriving silversmith practice, and also did a bit of dentistry on the side. As the city's lead health officer, Revere inspected ships entering Boston Harbor for signs of smallpox, yellow fever, and cholera, and he ordered quarantine when disease was found. He also was charged with cleaning up filth and waste, posting public warnings, and leading health education campaigns. He took his responsibilities seriously. He improved sanitation, and he ordered that so-called putrid puddles be drained. He demanded that the citizenry clean up the vaults of privies and mop up stagnant water in and around their homes. Revere had no idea that mosquitoes transmitted yellow fever. He didn't know about microbes. Germ theory did not yet exist. But he understood something more fundamental, that the environment in which people live affects their health. He practiced public health in its earliest form, surveillance, prevention, and protection, to benefit the public good. Massachusetts General Hospital was founded in 1811, with a radical premise for its time. A promise that medical care should be available regardless of ability to pay. When in distress, every man becomes our neighbor. The rallying cry in the circular letter that MGH founders Dr. John Collins Warren and Dr. James Jackson sent to the citizens of Boston, seeking funds to build a hospital to serve the growing city. At that time, those who could afford a physician were treated in their homes or in private offices. The poor, the sailors, servants, laborers, the homeless, were often sent to overcrowded almshouses or received no care at all. When Mass General opened its doors in 1821, it did so to serve the sick poor and society's most vulnerable. It did so to fulfill the bold promise that care should be guided by compassion, not circumstance. It did so because its founders believed that illness, not wealth, should determine who got treatment. Founding ideals are, by definition, only the beginning. An institution must hold true to those values. And sometimes it takes the single person willing to take significant risk to force that question into the open. And one of those people was Dr. Henry Ingersoll Bowditch. Henry Ingersoll Bowditch was the son of Nathaniel Bowditch, the famed mathematician and celestial navigator. Henry carved his own path as a physician, an abolitionist, and ultimately one of the founders of modern public health. Dr. Bowditch attended Harvard Medical School, spent a year at the MGH as a house physician, and then traveled to Paris to continue his medical studies. He returned to Boston to establish his own medical practice. As a young doctor in 1835, he witnessed an enraged mob dragging anti-slavery publisher and abolitionist William Lloyd Garrison through the streets of Boston, threatening to tar and feather him. Bowditch pleaded with the police to stop the violence, but they would not. In the end, it was the mayor of Boston who intervened, saving Garrison by placing him in jail for his own protection. For Dr. Bowditch, this was a moment of moral clarity. In his diary, he wrote that he was pledging his whole heart to the abolition of that monster slavery. This decision cost him. He lost patience. He lost friends. He lost community standing. He did not lose his conviction. That same resolve followed him into his medical practice. Counter to the hospital's founding values, the Mass General Trustees in 1841 adopted a policy barring Black patients from admission to the hospital. Dr. Bowditch, outraged by the action, challenged the system by attempting to admit a young Black girl with pneumonia. He was refused. His response was simple and decisive. He resigned from the hospital in protest, saying that he cannot remain in a situation that violated his view of justice. The bold act forced a reckoning at the MGH. The trustees understood that Bowditch was a gifted physician, as well as a figure of growing importance in American medicine. They didn't want to lose him. So they reversed course. The patient was admitted, and Dr. Bowditch remained at the hospital. By 1869, Dr. Bowditch's reputation as a leading physician, his pioneering work in public health, and his active moralistic advocacy for social reform made him an ideal pick to lead the newly formed Massachusetts State Board of Health, the first state health department in the nation. Under his leadership, Massachusetts embraced the then revolutionary idea that government had an obligation to protect health through sanitation, housing, water quality, and disease surveillance and prevention. His role gave him a platform on which to advocate for applying government power to help even the most marginalized citizens to live the healthiest life possible. It was Dr. Bowditch who embedded into the DNA of Massachusetts public health the idea that health is inseparable from justice. That tenet continues today as strongly as ever. Over the centuries, courage at Mass General was expressed in many ways. Sometimes it appeared as moral conviction, other times as scientific daring, and sometimes as the willingness to question practices so familiar that few imagined they could ever change. Again and again, this institution became a place where courage altered the course of medicine, and ultimately, the health of entire populations, the public's health. This is the place where, in 1846, the lead surgeon of the time, Dr. John Collins Warren, allowed a local dentist, William T.G. Morton, to come into the MGH operating theater and demonstrate what many considered an absurd idea, that surgery could be painless. Following the administration of anesthesia and the removal of a jaw tumor, the patient came to and reported that he felt no pain. And practically overnight, surgery was transformed from brutality to possibility. The modern era of anesthesia and surgery may have begun right here, but it was not just an ether-soaked sponge in the bottom of a glass inhaler that brought about this medical milestone. It was the courage of Dr. Warren and the curiosity of onlookers, mostly skeptical, who were willing to show up, consider the possibilities, and learn. That ether demonstration did more than change surgery. It changed expectations. Once medicine proved it could reduce suffering, new questions emerged about how to make care better, safer, kinder. These questions would echo through the generations that followed at the MGH, inspiring physicians who believe medicine must not only cure disease, but measure its outcomes, confront its failures, address the social realities shaping health itself. One of those physicians was Dr. Ernest Amory Codman, an MGH surgeon. Dr. Codman advanced an idea that many of his contemporaries considered deeply unsettling. Codman vigorously advocated for a system in which hospitals and surgeons would follow their patients after treatment. They'd measure outcomes. They would openly acknowledge their failures. His so-called end-result system called for tracking every patient for at least a year. Dr. Codman was ridiculed by his peers for even suggesting such an outrageous plan. The MGH dismissed his ideas flatly and in 1914 terminated his staff privileges. He then started his own hospital called the End Results Hospital to advance his performance measurement and quality improvement ideas. Dr. Codman's vision ultimately transformed medicine and public health. His work laid the foundation for the modern hospital standardization, patient safety, and outcomes research. It helped inspire the American College of Surgeons hospital standardization movement, which later evolved into today's joint commission. And Dr. Codman's insistence on accountability helped shape modern professional credentialing and quality oversight. In fact, his work inspired the creation of the professional licensing and regulatory boards that today are part of the Department of Public Health. Dr. Codman pushed forward the importance of measuring results in health care. But it was Dr. Richard Clark Cabot at the MGH who helped expand the definition of results. Dr. Codman's vision of the MGH. He looked beyond physiology and he saw a deeper truth. That social conditions like poverty, housing, work, and family circumstances shaped the health of patients. Acting on that insight, Dr. Cabot established the nation's first hospital-based social work program, integrating social workers directly into patient care at the MGH. Many physicians initially dismissed the idea as outside the proper scope of medicine. But Dr. Cabot understood that healing required more than diagnosis and treatment. It required addressing the conditions that made people sick in the first place. His insistence on dignity, on compassion, and on equity helped transform what it meant to truly care for a patient. And his legacy echoes today in every conversation about access to care, health equity, and the trust between communities and the health systems meant to serve them. Yet even as medicine was beginning to recognize the social forces shaping health, another reality emerged. Race limited who could participate in medicine itself and whose discoveries would be recognized. And it's here that we meet another extraordinary figure whose story connects the MGH, the Department of Public Health, and the still unfinished work of equity. Dr. William Hinton was a brilliant Black physician, the son of formerly enslaved people. He graduated with honors from Harvard Medical School in 1912. And of note, he supplemented his income during medical school by working in Dr. Cabot's clinical hematology lab. Dr. Hinton hoped to become a surgeon. But because of his race, he was unable to obtain any surgical residency or internship opportunities in Boston. Instead, he settled for research, working and teaching serological techniques in Harvard's Wasserman Laboratory, which focused on diagnosing syphilis. He was also a part-time volunteer assistant in the pathology laboratory at the MGH, where he performed autopsies on those whose deaths were likely related to syphilis. In 1915, the Wasserman Laboratory became part of the Massachusetts Department of Health, and Dr. Hinton was appointed chief of the Wasserman Lab and associate director of the state biological laboratories. He remained in this role until 1953, for nearly 40 years. From this laboratory, he changed medicine. He took what he learned in the lab and in the autopsy room, and he developed a test for syphilis, the Hinton test, a simple, quick, and precise diagnostic breakthrough considered the gold standard for decades. His work saved lives. But he also pushed so many other boundaries. He increased the breadth and scope of our state laboratories. He expanded career opportunities by creating a women-only laboratory technician school. He also holds the distinction of being the first Black full professor at Harvard. And yet, his career also stands as a stark reminder. Public health progress has often been achieved not because systems were equitable, but because individuals persisted despite unimaginable barriers to their success. That tension between scientific excellence and social exclusion runs through the history of medicine, and it continues to shape who trusts our institutions today. Before Dr. Hinton's achievements, there was another physician in Massachusetts who was already redefining both medicine and public health, though her story would remain largely hidden for generations. So I introduce you to another courageous Massachusetts public health pioneer, one who had no apparent formal connection to Massachusetts General Hospital or the Department of Public Health, yet whose work embodies the very principles both institutions believe in and have worked to advance. Her name is one we should all know. It is Dr. Rebecca Lee Crumpler. In 1864, as the Civil War rage, Dr. Crumpler became the first Black woman physician in the United States, an extraordinary achievement that happened right here in Massachusetts. Born in Delaware in 1831, Rebecca moved to Massachusetts in 1852, where she worked as a nurse in Charlestown, at a time when nursing itself had no formal training programs. Two physicians who observed her clinical skills and insights encouraged her to pursue medicine. This was remarkable in an era when very few women trained to be doctors and when most U.S. medical schools barred all Black students, male or female. Yet in 1860, she enrolled in the progressive New England Female Medical College, founded in 1848 as the first institution in the country to grant medical degrees to women. She graduated four years later, and after the Civil War with her new doctoress of medicine degree, Dr. Crumpler traveled to Richmond, Virginia, working with the Freedmen's Bureau to care for newly emancipated individuals who were navigating freedom amid profound poverty, trauma, and neglect. In Virginia, Dr. Crumpler experienced tremendous racism, sexism, and indignities from her male colleagues, and even from her patients. She spent much of her time caring for women and children, and she witnessed how the absence of food, safe housing, sanitation, and dignity profoundly shaped health outcomes. During her years in Virginia, she took extensive notes documenting living conditions, diseases, and overall health, as well as the well-being, disposition, and spirit of her patients. When Dr. Crumpler returned to Boston, she opened a practice in her home on Joy Street on Beacon Hill, just outside these walls, caring primarily for women and children who could not afford medical care. She continued her note-taking, recording both data and her impression of the effects of overcrowded tenements, rat infestations, contaminated water, and poor sanitation. She recognized that the conditions she saw in the poor neighborhoods of Boston mirrored those she had witnessed in the post-war South. Like Dr. Cabot-Actor Bird, she understood that disease could not be separated from the environments in which people lived. In 1883, after years of care, observation, and note-taking, she published a book of medical discourses, believed to be the first medical book written by a Black author in the United States. The book was a guide for mothers, families, and caregivers, offering practical guidance on pregnancy, nutrition, hygiene, infant care, and disease prevention. Her book has been called a forerunner of both Dr. Spock's Guide to Child Care and What to Expect When You're Expecting. Dr. Crumpler was, in every sense, ahead of her time, a physician who practiced community-centered care, documented social determinants of health, focused on prevention long before those ideas had caught on. And yet, for decades, her story was lost. No known photographs of her survive. Her legacy was recaptured several decades ago through her writings and through the work of dedicated individuals in Hyde Park, where she lived in her later years and where she was buried in an unmarked grave. Her grave was marked with a headstone in 2020, and her home on Joy Street is now a stop on the Boston Women's Heritage Trail. The work she began more than 150 years ago continues in ours today, protecting mothers and infants, strengthening communities, preventing disease, confronting inequities. inequities. I had not heard of Dr. Crumpler until recently, and as I learned more about this incredible pioneer, I could not help but wonder whether she and Dr. Bowditch ever crossed paths. What a formidable public health partnership that might have been. As medicine entered the 20th century, new scientific tools were transforming what physicians could see and understand about disease. germ theory reshaped medicine's foundations. Antibiotics promised cures once thought impossible. Hospitals became centers not only of care, but of discovery. Yet infectious disease remained one of humanity's greatest and most unpredictable threats, capable of crossing borders and overwhelming health systems. Of all medical specialties, infectious disease is the one most inseparable from public health. To me, as an infectious disease physician, the journey of public health is at the heart of this discipline. So let me tell you about a few of my MGH public health heroes. And I have to begin with Dr. Morton Swartz. What makes his story especially remarkable is that he was not trained as an infectious disease physician because the specialty did not yet exist when he was training. He was the founding chief of infectious diseases at Mass General, and he was one of the architects of the field itself. In 1953, Dr. Swartz served as MGH chief resident. He then went on to Johns Hopkins to pursue what he thought would be a career in research. But in 1955, Dr. Walter Bauer, then the MGH chair of medicine, called to ask him if he would consider coming back to build something new, something undefined. Dr. Swartz said yes, enthusiastically, stepping into a role that had no roadmap, no established identity, and big questions that needed answers. And that took courage. He became legendary as a diagnostician, a true medical detective. He had an uncanny ability to follow the faintest, most obscure clinical clues for clarity. He solved cases that had baffled entire teams. Physicians across specialties sought him out when the answers were elusive. So it was not a surprise that in 1976, when a mysterious and deadly illness struck attendees at an American Legion convention in Philadelphia, Dr. Schwartz was among the small group of experts called upon to investigate. He and that infectious disease A team helped unravel what we now know as Legionnaire's disease. He led the division here for 34 years, from 1956 to 1990. I never had the privilege of working directly with him. He died in 2013, just after I arrived here. But his presence remained unmistakable. You could feel it in the way people approached patients, in the questions they asked, in the humility with which uncertainty was treated. His influence lives, and still lives, in the division's culture, and in the humanism in medicine across the MGH. Brilliance alone is not what made Dr. Schwartz extraordinary. It was also his humanity, his interest in people as much as in pathogens. At a time when infectious disease was defining itself, he built a culture grounded in careful observation, rigorous thinking, and deep compassion. He was generous with his time, meticulous with his reasoning, and profoundly kind. He taught generations of physicians that infectious disease is not only about medicine and microbes. It's about listening to patients, to communities, and to what the data are quietly revealing before a crisis fully unfolds. And that is public health at its core. The leaders of the MGH infectious disease division who followed him, including Dr. Steve Calderwood and Dr. Rochelle Walensky, carried forward that tradition. Each demonstrated in their own way that infectious disease medicine does not stop at the bedside. It extends outward, into communities, into policy, into public service. The infectious disease work of this hospital is necessarily linked to the public health work across the Commonwealth. When Dr. Calderwood succeeded Dr. Schwartz as chief in 1990, it was a time when the HIV AIDS epidemic was confronting physicians not only with scientific uncertainty, but with fear, stigma, and extraordinary human suffering. Under Dr. Calderwood's leadership, the division navigated this era with both scientific rigor and compassion. Even as treatments were evolving from palliative care to highly active antiretroviral therapy, those with HIV continued to be marginalized. Physicians were called upon to advocate, to comfort, and to stand beside those patients whose society too often turned away from. Dr. Calderwood strengthened the division's commitment to science while reinforcing the obligation not only to understand illness, but to confront the social forces that shape who becomes sick and who receives care. He recruited the top minds of the day to take on the disease. Physician scientists who embodied all aspects of that term. Astute researchers who were pioneering and courageous and empathetic clinicians who sat at the bedside at all hours of day and night. These are the individuals who became my teachers and my mentors, my guides that connected the work of infectious disease in the hospital to the work of public health in our communities. The tradition of compassionate leadership continued under Dr. Rochelle Walensky, who succeeded Dr. Calderwood as chief in 2017. Her career reflects the increasingly visible overlap of academic medicine and public health leadership. Rochelle, Dr. Walensky, is a gifted clinician. She is a world-class researcher. She is a superbly talented communicator. And she is filled with the compassion and humanism that traces back to Dr. Schwartz. She led the division during an era when infectious diseases and public health once again moved to the center of public life. Her work focused not only on advancing HIV care and outcomes, but on understanding how health systems, policy, and access shape survival itself, bringing data and humanity together in powerful and meaningful ways. And then along came COVID-19. Dr. Walensky was integral in leading the response at the MGH, as well as advising officials locally, nationally, and internationally. In late 2020, she got the phone call of a lifetime. She was asked to serve as director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention during one of the most challenging public health crises in our modern history. She stepped into this role boldly and purposefully, a role defined by science, but also by scrutiny, uncertainty, and immense responsibility. That decision required courage of a different kind, the courage to lead in the brightest, most intense spotlight imaginable, where every decision is debated in real time, and where science must compete with fear, misinformation, and politics. I had the honor and the privilege to watch Rochelle lead, to see her courage up close. I doubt I will ever see someone in my lifetime with the strength and moral clarity that I saw in Rochelle during her time in CDC. In her actions, she changed the course of public health, not just for the country, but for the world. And a little bit closer to home, she changed the course of my life. And for that, I am forever grateful. Across these generations of leadership, a common thread emerges. The understanding that infectious disease medicine carries a responsibility to be diligent, to look under every rock, to think about every possibility, and to be open-minded and willing to consider something new, maybe even something terrifying. In 2022, my friend, my colleague, my mentor here at Mass General, Dr. Nestle Vasquez, encountered a patient whose symptoms did not quite fit expected patterns. The patient was tested and retested for likely infections, and all the tests came back negative. He didn't respond to antibiotics or antiviral medications, and the team was stumped. Progress in medicine often begins with a detail that may be easily overlooked. In this case, it was the tiny dimple on the blister that had formed on the patient's skin. Dr. Vasquez noticed it. Through careful clinical insight, determination, and a willingness to think outside the box, she identified the first recognized case of MPOX in the United States. And what folded after that makes me particularly proud. The suspicion of MPOX ignited an immediate partnership involving the team at the MGH, the team from the Department of Public Health, and the National Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which happened to be where I was working at the time. Clinicians, laboratories, staff, epidemiologists, public health leaders moved swiftly and collaboratively, tracing the source, confirming the diagnosis, and mobilizing a response. This was the nation's public health system working exactly as it was meant to work, seamlessly, thoughtfully, and with a shared commitment to protecting the public. That moment, when clinical insight became coordinated public health action, also reflects another lesson, that protecting health starts in communities. In 1965, right here in Massachusetts, physicians Jack Geiger and Dr. Count Gibson opened the nation's first community health center in Dorchester. The Geiger-Gibson Community Health Center was built on a simple idea that health care should exist where people live, learn, work, and dream. The center recognized that health is shaped as much by neighborhood conditions, trust, and relationships as by diagnosis and treatment. The MGH understood this concept right away. In 1968, it opened its Charlestown Health Care Center, becoming part of the first wave of institutions to embrace community-based care. Health centers were never meant to be merely just clinics. They became gathering places, anchors in the fabric of neighborhoods, places where care is continuous, culturally grounded, and trusted because it's local. And that kind of trust, built over decades, is one of public health's most powerful tools. When health care is rooted in community, it cannot ignore the forces that shape community health, safety, and well-being. Sadly, one of those forces that cannot be ignored is, too often, violence. And that realization has led to efforts to not just treat the medical effects of violence, but to confront it as a preventable public health challenge. At Mass General, my good friend, Dr. Hannah Sachs, a primary care physician, along with Dr. Peter Masiakos, a pediatric trauma surgeon, established the Gun Violence Prevention Center. For Dr. Sachs, this work was deeply personal. In 2012, her young cousin was killed in the Sandy Hook school shooting. Out of unimaginable loss came determination, a belief that medicine and public health could not remain silent in the face of preventable harm. The center approaches firearm injury not as a political issue, but as a public health crisis, grounded in data, prevention, clinical care, and community partnership. Its work ranges from simulation training that helps clinicians counsel patients about firearm safety to research examining the profound ripple effects gun violence has on families and communities long after the headlines fade. It reflects a fundamental public health truth that prevention is not passive. It requires courage. The courage to name a problem, to study it honestly, and to work collaboratively towards solutions even when the path forward is uncomfortable. The willingness to confront difficult realities and to rethink who medicine is designed to serve is something I experienced personally during my time at MGH. I chose to train in infectious disease with a clear vision of the patients I expected to take care of. I believed my career would focus largely on HIV care and prevention among gay and bisexual men. But medicine has a way of teaching humility and of revealing needs we may not have initially seen. In treating patients at risk for and living with HIV, I learned that those most disproportionately affected were transgender women. This population was not comfortable, not welcome, in traditional medical settings. many did not keep up with or even seek care. Most had experienced discrimination, misunderstanding, judgment, or outright rejection from the healthcare system. Some had gone years without primary care. The barrier was not medicine itself. It was trust. So we asked the question, what would it look like to build a program that was grounded in trust? We talked with a lot of people did a lot of research. And in 2018, we opened the Mass General Hospital Transgender Health Program. To be successful, this initiative would have to involve much more than just setting up a nice medical clinic. It was about changing culture. We needed to teach a venerable academic medical institution what it meant to welcome, care for, and affirm transgender patients. It was a daunting task. And to do it would require support from the very top. We were able to establish the Transgender Health Program because of the courage, leadership, and example of Dr. Peter Slavin, then President of the MTH, and Dr. Katrina Armstrong, then Chair of Medicine. They listened to us as we described the unusual idea. They understood that this program would not be financially lucrative, but they knew it would serve a population that had been too often overlooked by society and by medicine itself. They saw in this work the founding values of this institution, that when in distress, every man, every person, becomes our neighbor. And they said yes. They provided space, they committed resources, and more important, through their actions, they reinforced their commitment to the principle of health equity, that health care must reach those who have been left out. They opened those doors because it was the right thing to do. And that took courage. And that brings us to where we are right now. Across the country, at the highest levels, we are seeing attacks on science, on expertise, and on the idea that protecting health is a shared responsibility. We see misinformation spreading faster than evidence. We see data questioned, institutions weakened, and public servants asked to do harder work. This is a crisis. It's a crisis of trust. And trust, once fractured, takes patience, humility, and time to rebuild. But history offers us some helpful perspective. When we look back, we see public health making its greatest advances in the toughest times. When new treatments were resisted, when sanitation practices were challenged, when vaccination sparked fear and controversy long before social media. What carried public health forward was persistence. It was humility. And it was the profound belief that every life has equal value. That belief guides our work every day at the Department of Public Health. Strengthening surveillance, expanding access to care, addressing mental health and substance use, confronting violence, and working alongside communities where trust must be earned and demonstrated again and again and again. The work right now is hard. It's maybe harder than it's been in a generation. And that is why it matters so much. I tell our staff at every possible turn that this is not the time for public health to freeze with uncertainty or to retreat and wait for a friendlier time. This is a moment when public health can shine. It's when public health must shine. Because when we consider the people who we've talked about tonight, Onesimus and Cotton Mather and Zebediah Boylston, George Washington and Paul Revere, Henry Bowditch, William Hinton and Rebecca Crumpler, and when we see that same spirit carried through Mort Swartz, Rochelle Walensky, Nestle Bazgoth, Hannah Sachs, we begin to notice something. None of them cared how history would remember them. They were not trying to be pioneers. They were simply trying to do what was right in front of them to relieve suffering. To follow the evidence. To protect people others overlooked. What they did wasn't easy. What they did was necessary in the moment. Public health is different from medicine in that it asks us to care for people we may never meet. It asks us to prevent tragedies that no one will ever see or know about. It asks us to make decisions in public under scrutiny, often in moments of fear and uncertainty. And the question before us right now is the same question that has been asked for centuries.
